subject: science
topic: Antibiotics are creating 'super-bugs' that threaten to end modern medicine
angle: Antibiotic use and environmental contaminants drive the evolution of resistance through mechanisms like gene duplication, horizontal gene transfer, and independent evolution in specific lineages.
title: The Evolution of Resistance

hooks.text: Can bacteria learn to survive every medicine?
You assume medicine kills bacteria. The evidence shows they adapt.
Your consumption fuels the evolution of super-bugs.
A single drop of water in a sterile room.

reveal.headline: Bacteria evolve resistance in nearly every lineage.
reveal.body: When exposed to specific antimicrobial peptides, 22 out of 24 lineages of Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas fluorescens independently developed heritable resistance.

explain.headline: Selection drives genetic duplication.
explain.body: Antibiotic use can cause bacteria to duplicate their resistance genes. These duplicated genes are highly present in bacteria found in humans and livestock.

matters.headline: Resistance is an environmental byproduct.
matters.body: That may be why microscopic pollutants like microplastics and chemicals influence how bacteria evolve and spread resistance across our shared environment.

example.headline: The water in your sink.
example.body: You turn on the tap and watch the water flow over the basin. It carries microscopic remnants of modern life.

question.headline: How much of your environment is rewriting bacterial life?

stat.label: lineages of bacteria that independently evolved resistance

claims.text: 22/24 lineages of Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas fluorescens independently evolved heritable mechanisms of resistance to pexiganan when propagated in medium supplemented with this antimicrobial peptide for 600-700 generations.
claims.quote: In this selection experiment, 22/24 lineages of Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas fluorescens independently evolved heritable mechanisms of resistance to pexiganan, an analogue of magainin, when propagated in medium supplemented with this antimicrobial peptide for 600-700 generations.

claims.text: Emerging contaminants such as endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs), persistent organic pollutants (POPs), and microplastics also significantly influence the emergence, evolution, and dissemination of bacterial antimicrobial resistance.
claims.quote: In addition to antibiotics themselves, emerging contaminants such as endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs), persistent organic pollutants (POPs), and microplastics also significantly influence the emergence, evolution, and dissemination of bacterial antimicrobial resistance.

claims.text: Antibiotic selection can drive the evolution of duplicated antibiotic resistance genes through MGE transposition.
claims.quote: Modeling and experiments show that antibiotic selection can drive the evolution of duplicated antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) through MGE transposition.

claims.text: Duplicated antibiotic resistance genes are highly enriched in bacteria isolated from humans and livestock.
claims.quote: Duplicated ARGs are highly enriched in bacteria isolated from humans and livestock.

claims.text: The selective pressures caused by increased use and misuse of antimicrobials in medicine and livestock production have accelerated the overall selection of resistant bacteria.

verdict: The evidence confirms that antibiotic use and environmental factors accelerate the selection and spread of resistance genes, including the evolution of resistance to novel antimicrobial peptides.
caveat: While many mechanisms are identified, there is an urgent need to further investigate the specific mechanisms of antimicrobial-induced horizontal transfer.
caption:
Antibiotics are driving the evolution of resistant bacteria. 
Research shows that antibiotic use, livestock production, and environmental contaminants like microplastics accelerate the selection of resistance genes. Scientists still need to investigate the specific mechanisms of antimicrobial-induced horizontal transfer.
How do you think our environment is changing the biology of bacteria?
